## Learning Outcomes

- Explain what happens at each stage of the **fetch, decode,
  execute, store** cycle.

- Use a simple **instruction set** to write some assembler programs for
  a toy computer.

- Go further: write some assembler programs for a real instruction set!

- Give the main difference between RICS and CISC architecture, stating their advantages and disadvantages as well as situations in which each is best used.

- State **Moore's law** and discuss whether it is still relevant today.

## Recap: Harvard architecture

:::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: cell-output-display
![](../assets/02-harvard.svg){fig-align="center"
fig-alt="diagram of Harvard architecture showing the same components as Von Neumann, but with separate memory and separate buses for instructions and data"
width="60%"}
:::
::::

::: notes
Recall the control unit, arithmetic logic unit, input and output.
Harvard architecture has separate memory for programs and data, and a
separate bus. This meant there was less contention as instructions and
data could be accessed simultaneously, but the machine was less
flexible, e.g., the program memory may not be full when data memory is,
but we cannot use the free space in the program memory for additional
data. This architecture commonly used in embedded systems, and
mainframes.
:::

## The Von Neumann Architecture

:::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: cell-output-display
![](../assets/02-vna.svg){fig-align="center"
fig-alt="diagram of Von Neumann architecture showing five components"
width="55%"}
:::
::::

::: notes
Same components: control unit, arithmetic logic unit, input and output.
In the Harvard architecture, data and instructions are stored in the
**same** memory. A single memory bus can be a bottleneck, and concerns
were raised about security (e.g., a program can write to any location in
memory, including modifying the instructions. Simpler and more flexible.
This is the architecture found in most desktop computers today.
:::

# The CPU

## Components

:::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: cell-output-display
![](../assets/03-cpu.svg){fig-align="center"
fig-alt="diagram of Von Neumann architecture showing five components described on the next page"
width="50%"}
:::
::::

## The CPU

- A program, written in assembler, is a sequence of **instructions**.

- The program is loaded into *main memory* so that the next instruction
  is in the next memory address:

## The CPU

  the **program counter (PC)** points to the memory location of the
  current instruction.

## The CPU

- The current instruction itself is stored in the **instruction register
  (IR)**.

## The CPU

- The **control unit** decodes the instruction and tells the
  **arithmetic logic unit (ALU)** which operations to perform.

## The CPU

- The CPU has a small number of **registers** (R1, R2, and R3 on the
  picture) to store intermediate values.

- There is also a small amount of very fast memory, the **cache**,
  located either on or very near the CPU.

## The Fetch, decode, execute store Cycle

A CPU goes through **four stages** to run an instruction:

:::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: cell-output-display
![](../assets/03-fetch.svg){fig-align="center"
fig-alt="shows four stages, fetch decode execute and store, linked in a loop"
width="30%"}
:::
::::

## Fetch

::::: columns
::: column
- First stage of the cycle.

- **Program counter** points to the memory address of the next
  instruction.

- Retrieve the next instruction from memory and store it in the
  **instruction register**.

- Increment the **program counter** to point to the next instruction.

:::
::: column
:::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: cell-output-display
![](../assets/03-fetch-f.svg){fig-align="center"
fig-alt="shows four stages, fetch decode execute and store, linked in a loop"
width="60%"}
:::
::::
:::
:::::

## Decode

::::: columns
::: column

- The **control unit** reads the current instruction in the
  **instruction register**.

- The **control unit** determines which operation(s) to perform.

- If the instruction has *operands* the **control unit** initiates
  additional fetches to retrieve these from memory.

:::
::: column
:::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: cell-output-display
![](../assets/03-fetch-d.svg){fig-align="center"
fig-alt="shows four stages, fetch decode execute and store, linked in a loop"
width="60%"}
:::
::::
:::

The CPU is now **ready to execute the instruction**.
:::::

## Execute

::::: columns
::: column

- The stage at which **operations are performed**.

- The ALU performs the decoded operation with its operands.

  In more advanced CPUs may have special-purpose hardware, e.g., a
  **floating point unit**.

- Instruction may *load* data from memory into a **register**.

- May perform a *jump* (e.g., conditional or loop) -- **program
  counter** is set to point to a different instruction.

:::
::: column
:::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: cell-output-display
![](../assets/03-fetch-e.svg){fig-align="center"
fig-alt="shows four stages, fetch decode execute and store, linked in a loop"
width="60%"}
:::
::::

Any return value is stored in a **register**.
Ready for the next stage...
:::
:::::


# Store

::::: columns
::: column

- Any computed values currently saved in a **register** are *stored* in
  the **main memory**.

- Final stage in the cycle.

- The cycle is now repeated.

:::
::: column
:::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: cell-output-display
![](../assets/03-fetch-s.svg){fig-align="center"
fig-alt="shows four stages, fetch decode execute and store, linked in a loop"
width="60%"}
:::
::::
:::
:::::

## Interrupt

- Occasionally, the CPU receives an **interrupt signal**.

- The CPU immediately stops executing the current instruction and
  **jumps** to an *interrupt service routine*.

- The *interrupt service routine* is just another set of instructions
  stored in memory.

- The CPU executes these instructions as usual, then jumps back to the
  instruction it was previously working on.

- If the instruction was interrupted halfway through, then the CPU must
  restart it from the beginning.

## The Little man Computer

::: columns
::: column

- Simple model of a **Von Neumann architecture** computer.

- Imagine a "Little Man" trapped inside a locked mail room.

- The mail room has **100 mailboxes** labelled 00-99, each of which can
  hold a 3 decimal digit *instruction* or *data*.

:::
::: column
:::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: cell-output-display
![](../assets/03-mailroom.jpg){fig-align="center"
fig-alt="photograph of a mailroom with mailboxes on the wall"
width="60%"}
:::
::::

- Input is received via an **inbox** and output returned via an
  **outbox**.

- There is a work area with a simple addition and subtraction, the
  **accumulator**.

- There is a **program counter** which tells the *Little Man* from which
  address to fetch the next instruction.

:::
::::

## How it works

1.  The Little Man checks the **program counter** and retrieves the
    instruction at the specified address.

2.  The **program counter** is incremented so that it points to the
    address (mailbox) containing the next instruction.

3.  Little Man **decodes** the instruction.

- **Op-code**: number from 000-999 which tells the Little Man what
  operation to perform.
- If data is required, its mailbox **address** is included in the
  instruction.

1.  If required, data is **fetched** from the mailbox referred in the
    instruction.

2.  **Execute** the instruction.

3.  *Branch* (change the value in the program counter) or *store* the
    result of the instruction.

4.  **Repeat** or **halt**.

## Instructions {.smaller}

::: columns
::: column

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------
        Name              Code                    Description
  ----------------- ----------------- ------------------------------------
        `ADD`             $1XX$       **Add** value in mailbox $XX$ to the
                                          value in the *accumulator*.

        `SUB`             $2XX$        **Subtract** value in mailbox $XX$
                                      fro the value in the *accumulator*.

        `STA`             $3XX$       **Store** value in *accumulator* in
                                                  mailbox $XX$

        `LDA`             $5XX$       **Load** value in mailbox $XX$ into
                                               the *accumulator*

        `BRA`             $6XX$            **Unconditionally go to**
                                          instruction in mailbox $XX$
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------

:::
::: column

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------
        Name              Code                    Description
  ----------------- ----------------- ------------------------------------
        `BRZ`             $7XX$       **Conditionally go to** instruction
                                           in mailbox $XX$ **if** the
                                              *accumulator* is $0$

        `BRP`             $8XX$       **Conditionally go to** instruction
                                           in mailbox $XX$ **if** the
                                             *accumulator* is $> 0$

        `INP`             $901$         Read **input** from the *inbox*,
                                         store it in the *accumulator*.

        `OUT`             $902$            Write **output** from the
                                         *accumulator* to the *outbox*.

        `HLT`             $000$          **Halt** -- stop the program.
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------
:::
:::

## Assembler {.smaller}

::: columns
::: column

- **Mnemonics** (3-letter codes) are often used, e.g., `ADD`,

  Instead of the 3-digit **op-code**, e.g., $1XX$, since they are easier
  for the programmer to remember.

- A program is a sequence of instructions, which are executed in order
  -- *imperative programming*.

- **Labels** (similar to variables) are used instead of memory address
  numbers.

:::
::: column

### Add two numbers

    INP # store value from inbox in accumulator
    STA FIRST # store accumulator value in FIRST mailbox
    INP
    STA SECOND
    LDA FIRST # load first number into accumulator
    ADD SECOND # ADD SECOND value to accumulator
    OUT # output the value of accumulator
    FIRST DAT # reserves a data mailbox
    SECOND DAT

- `DAT` reserves a *labelled* mailbox for data.

:::
:::

## Labels, constants and jumps {.smaller}

::: columns
::: column

- **Labels** are used to refer to *mailbox locations*.

- Since instructions are stored in mailboxes, they can be labelled, too.

  E.g., `loop OUT` labels the location of the `OUT` instruction as
  `loop`.

- **Branches** need the memory address of the instruction to go to -- we
  can use labels.

  E.g., `BNP loop` goes to `loop` as long as the *accumulator* value is
  positive.

- A labelled mailbox can be **initialised** to a constant.

  E.g., `one DAT 1` initialises the mailbox labelled `one` to $1$.

:::
::: column

         INP
    loop OUT
         SUB one
         STA count
         BRP loop
         HLT
    1
    one DAT 1
    count DAT

:::
:::

## Exercise: little man programming {.smaller}

- Go to <https://www.101computing.net/LMC/>

  Play with the simulator, try some of the example programs.

- Code the following programs:

  - **Difference**: User *inputs* two numbers, $A$ and $B$. Program
    calculates their *difference*, $A - B$.
  - **Count up**: User *inputs* a number, $N$, program should count up
    from $0$ to $N$.
  - **Multiplication**: There is no multiplication instruction, but
    $A \cdot B = \underbrace{A \cdot A \cdots A}_{B \text{ times}}$.
    Implement multiplication.

  You may want to plan your code on paper, like the EDSAC programmers.

# Instruction set architectures

## Instruction set architectures

- Each processor architecture has its own **instruction set**:

  A set of *op-codes* which the control unit interprets as instructions.

- There are two main types of instruction set architecture

  - **RISC**: reduced instruction set computer, and
  - **CISC**: complex instruction set computer.

## History

- Up to the early 80's, more instructions were being added to
  processors.

- Designers wanted to **mimic high-level programming languages**.

  One CPU instruction should be one line of source code.

- Offload more work onto the hardware.

- Produce shorter programs (fewer total instructions) to conserve
  memory.

## History

- In the early 80's, the idea of creating a smaller and simple set of
  instructions was proposed.

- Aim was to make designing and building a CPU **easier**, **cheaper**
  and, therefore, **faster**.

- Term **RISC** coined by David Patterson, a researcher at UC Berkeley.

## RISC: reduced instruction set computer

Small, simple set of instructions, e.g., as found in the Little Man
computer.

- Processor can execute **exactly one** instruction per cycle.

- Instructions are a **fixed length** (fixed number of bits).

- Can only manipulate values **stored in CPU registers**.

- RISC chips are simple to design and cheap to build.

- Used in ARM-based chips, found in microcontrollers (Arduino, Raspberry
  Pi) and smartphones.

  Also used in IBM Power processors (used in mainframes and servers).

## CISC: complex instruction set computing

Large number of instructions, some performing more complicated
operations -- intended to correspond to statements in a high-level
programming language.

- **Variable-length** instructions.

- May take **multiple clock cycles** to execute an instruction.

- Able to manipulate values **directly in main memory**.

- CISC chips are complex, with special-purpose hardware, and are more
  expensive to build.

- Found in most PCs -- the x86 architecture.

## Simple example: RISC vs CISC

Suppose we want to *increment* a value stored in *main memory*.

::: columns-2
## CISC architecture

- A **single instruction**:

  `ADD mem one`

  - Retrieves the value from memory,
  - Adds one to it,
  - Writes back to memory.

### CISC architecture

- **Three separate instructions**:

      LDA mem
      ADD one
      STA mem
:::

# A little more history

## Second-generation of computers

- Recall that early computers, e.g., EDSAC, used vacuum tubes
  (thermionic valves).

- These were **bulky**, **unreliable**, **generated lots of heat** and
  **required lots of energy** to run.

- In the late 1950s, computers began to use **electronic circuit
  boards** made out of transistors instead.

- These computers were popular until the late 1960s.

## First transistor computer

::::: columns
::: column

- Developed at the University of Manchester

- Working prototype in November **1953**,

  had **92 transistors** and **950 diodes**.

- Full-size version was operational in **1955**

  had **200 transistors**, **1300 diodes** and consumed **150W** of
  power.

- Early transistors were unreliable. Average error-free runtime was
  **1.5 hours**.

- **Not fully transistorised** as it still used vacuum tubes in its
  clock.

:::
::: column

:::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: cell-output-display
![](../assets/03-tradic.jpg){fig-align="center"
fig-alt="TRADIC computer" width="30%"}
:::
::::

- **TRADIC** transistor computer, developed at Bell Labs, released
  January 1954.

  Used a single high-power output vacuum tube amplifier to obtain a
  **1MHz clock speed**.

:::
:::::

## Fully transistorised computer

- Harwell Cadet, 1955. **58KHz** clock speed.

- Prototype IBM 604 Transistor calculator.

- IBM 608, released April 1955 is considered to be the first
  **commercial fully solid-state** transistor computer.

## Third generation computers

- Widely used from the mid 60s to early 70s.

- Used **integrated circuits** (ICs)

- An IC is a single *chip* containing all transistors, resistors,
  capacitors, diodes and connections needed to operate.

- Invented by Jack Kilby in 1958, an electrical engineer working at
  Texas Instruments.

  Awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000.

- Faster and more reliable than second generation.

- Reduced computing time from **micro** seconds to **nano** seconds.

- Computers were becoming more **compact**, **affordable** and **easy to
  use** with high-level programming languages and mouse and keyboard
  instead of punched cards.

# Moore's Law

## Moore's "Law"

- Prediction made by Gordon Moore, co-founder of Intel, in 1965:

  "Number of transistors per chip doubles every two years."

::: notes
Note that it's not a "law" as in "law of physics". More of a prediction
which has remained (mostly) true.
:::

## Moore's Law Graph

:::: {.cell fag.align="center"}
::: cell-output-display
![](../assets/03-moore.png){fig-alt="A semi-log plot of transistor counts for microprocessors against dates of introduction, nearly doubling every two years"
width="95%"}
:::
::::

## Dennard scaling

- Stated in a 1974 paper co-authored by Robert H. Dennard:

  "As transistors get smaller, their power density stays constant --
  power use stays in proportion with area."

- If a transistor is **30%** smaller, then its power consumption is
  **30%** less.

- An IC of fixed size with **twice** the number of transistors consumes
  **the same power**.

- Allowed manufacturers to **significantly increase clock speed**
  without increase power consumption.

## Dennard scaling

::::: columns
::: column 

- Appears to have broken down since 2006.

- Since 2016 the number of transistors per chip is still growing, but
  more slowly.

- As transistors get smaller, current leakage and heat production is
  more problematic.

:::
::: column

:::: {.cell fag.align="center"}
::: cell-output-display
![](../assets/03-powerwall.png){fig-alt="graph illustrating power wall"
width="95%"}
:::
::::

- We see clock speed plateau -- as clack speed increases it becomes more
  difficult to cool the chip.

  This is called the *power wall*.
:::
:::::

## Exercise: Moore's law

Discuss:

- Is Moore's law still true today?

::: notes
- There have been many predictions of the death of Moore's law.

- We are no longer able to **double** the number of transistors per
  chip.

- Transistors are still getting smaller and more tightly packed, but
  progress is becoming slower.

:::


# RISC V

## RISC V

- Open source instruction set architecture, open standard for processor design.
- Reduced Instruction Set Architecture version 5
- Load --- store architecture, using IEEE 754 for floating point.
- 32 and 64 bit address spaces, wip 128 bit
